title: Primary and Unique Constraints
learning_outcomes: Describe the purpose and main terms of Primary and Unique Constraints.
Use or interpret an appropriate PostgreSQL example connected to defining a primary key.
Identify one edge case and select a safe way to verify the expected result.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on Primary and Unique Constraints. Its primary job is to help you define and evolve schemas with constraints, generated values and changes that are safe for populated tables. The listed PDF subtopics define the coverage expected here; work through them in order and connect each one to an example, edge case and checkable result.
content.why_it_matters: This topic matters because PostgreSQL systems must preserve correct results as data grows and more sessions or services interact with it. Practicing primary and unique constraints teaches you to make assumptions explicit, apply the right SQL or operational tool, and verify behavior instead of relying on a demonstration that only worked once.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Keep the problem small: define and evolve schemas with constraints, generated values and changes that are safe for populated tables. A PostgreSQL feature should be chosen for the semantics it provides, not just because it is available. Before executing a change, state the inputs, expected output and boundary conditions. The example below is intentionally small enough to inspect; it illustrates the idea but is not a substitute for a test against your schema and PostgreSQL version.

items.title: Defining a primary key
items.text: Choose an identifier that is stable and enforceable; test both duplicate and missing-value cases.

items.title: Unique constraints
items.text: Choose an identifier that is stable and enforceable; test both duplicate and missing-value cases.

items.title: Composite uniqueness
items.text: Choose specialized types where their operators directly help the domain; document boundaries and constraints.

items.title: Nullable columns and uniqueness
items.text: Treat NULL as unknown or absent: use IS NULL/IS NOT NULL and review how expressions and aggregates handle it.

items.title: Indexes associated with constraints
items.text: Match the index method and operator class to real query predicates, then compare the plan and write/storage costs.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Primary and Unique Constraints
content_blocks.code:
CREATE TABLE products (
  id bigint GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  sku text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name text NOT NULL,
  price numeric(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (price >= 0),
  available boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true
);
content_blocks.expected_output: Creates a products table with an identity primary key and constraints for SKU uniqueness, required fields and nonnegative prices.
content_blocks.safety_note: Schema-changing example; use migrations and review constraints against existing records.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in a disposable database. Check the database version and inspect the resulting table definition.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For a read-only SELECT or inspection command, no reset is needed. For DDL/DML, use a disposable database; capture the starting state, run the example, inspect the result, and ROLLBACK or drop the lab objects as appropriate. Do not use production data or credentials.

content_blocks.title: Practical checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Version note: PostgreSQL 18.6 is the primary reference. PostgreSQL 19 beta/development features are not assumed to be stable.

task: Create a short practice artifact for “Primary and Unique Constraints”: explain its goal, show one example linked to “Defining a primary key”, state the expected result, and include one edge/failure case and verification method. Use a disposable database or static artifact as appropriate.
hints: Start with the listed subtopics, especially “Defining a primary key”, and describe the expected behavior in your own words.
Run or inspect the smallest example that demonstrates the behavior; do not add unrelated features before it is verified.
When the result surprises you, capture the exact SQL/error, check version and permissions, and change one assumption at a time.
expected_output: A reviewable note or query for Primary and Unique Constraints, with an explanation of “Defining a primary key”, expected behavior, and a documented edge-case check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying the example without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Object names, data types, privileges, extensions and data distribution affect database behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: List schema/version assumptions and test with a tiny synthetic dataset first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a single successful query as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: A happy-path result does not test invalid input, concurrent sessions, permissions, recovery or query performance.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one negative/edge case and record the evidence that confirms the expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Making a production change directly from a lesson.
common_mistakes.why: DDL, data updates, role changes and operational commands can affect data or availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use an isolated lab, reviewed migration, least privilege, rollback/recovery plan and a second-person review for production.

summary: Primary and Unique Constraints fits into the broader goal to define and evolve schemas with constraints, generated values and changes that are safe for populated tables.
Use the curriculum subtopics as a completeness checklist: Defining a primary key, Unique constraints, Composite uniqueness.
State the schema/version assumptions and verify one normal case plus an edge case before trusting the result.
